12 o'clock playing quadrilles. 12 o'clock, first figure, yeah. 11.30, 11.30, first figure. Yeah, first figure, yeah. 11.30, first figure, first figure, And they all rest there.

Big Easy. Where was that?

That's in the Grittner. Oh. Go over to Grittner and play the Big Easy. Now like the first... Big Easy and they come clean. Big Easy and they come clean. See? And then they had another one over there called the number 12. See? Well they give dances every Saturday night. They hold about 50 people I believe. And they made money. You get a glass of beer like that for nickel, wine for nickel, sell you dinner. They made money. And everybody was happy. Well the first band we had a trumpet player called Harrison Gougie. You remember Gougie? His old daddy had that Schumacher shop back on Duvern Street. See? Absolutely. Yeah. See? Harrison could play everything he see but he couldn't play in nothing, so he don't listen to look at the music. He was just a straight shot. He just learnt my music. See? He didn't have no... No. He didn't know...

Oh. Harrison Gougie. I know. That's what I'm saying. That's just what I'm saying right now. That's just what I'm saying right now. I'm glad you brought man because we could think of some people. Then we have another Creole boy called Ogin. Ogin? Ogin. From way down on, Mary Sugar refiner played trumpet, hold his head down and played some of the sweet... He wasn't no high note man but he played some of the nicest stuff with the old ugly hooker guy. Oh. Yeah. They don't write with those guys. They don't know. Yeah, nobody's heard of. You see, you see now, I should write a book myself. Should've done write a book. Yeah, he's good. He knows people. You see, we're getting back to the guys who work in the district. You see. Now Bunk, Bunk got so bad around, it ruined Bunk when he went with the Eagle band. When he was down there with the Superior band down there with the Creole boys it was very nice. For months and months Bunk didn't go home, sleep on the pool table, time to go play.
Yeah.

He never, all his trouble that Bunk ever got into was himself. Himself. See, just drinking. And Bunk, just didn't start drinking. Bunk was drinking for a long time. Bunk left New Orleans about 1910 and I didn't see Bunk no more until 1937 and I didn't know Bunk. See, I know the Bunk but I didn't know Bunk when I seen him, you know, at all of me. And Bunk would've known me until he asked Louie who is that. See, he, cause you know when you go in the towns and the names up there, it says, Louie, who's that boy, I don't know, it says George, I don't know, it says George, I don't know, I said, now me, Bunk. Louie said, Bunk, and he went over to see, he didn't have enough teeth on his head.
Louie told me about that too, he met him in New Iberia, he came and sat there with the

band. Yeah, sat there. And the boys out here, one of the boys I'm trying to find out, see I haven't seen him any yet, they got together out here and bought Bunk his horn. The first horn, when they found him, they went down there on that plantation where he was driving the truck, give him his horn, see. Give credit where Louie didn't give him that horn.
Oh, that's right.

Louie didn't give him that horn, see. Louie give a horn to the fishers, I told you about that the other night, I wanted that to go in there, but the valet forgot to put the horn on the running board of that bus and it bounced off last we see it was floating out in that river.

Yeah, when was that? Did that horn run over and all that? That was around 1937 or 1936. It didn't run over, this fellow off that bridge. That bridge had bounced and it bounced and went right over. old boy went.

That bridge crossed that river from Baltimore, Philadelphia to Baltimore. And what was Louie, was that Louie's own horn or what about the story of the story? Yeah, it's the own horn, see. Rozeal.

And Joe Johnson, the trumpet player, had been playing guitar?
Yeah. Roy Palmer too.
Yeah I knew that Roy had played a different instrument.

Roy played guitar, see. Roy was our trumpet player for a long time then. Roy got on trombone. And we played, we played little things. I went down and play that Sunday, and then they started to rave about me playing, then we got this little band and we called rehearsal, we had rehearsal twice a week. Our rehearsal was like a party. And if you know the cop on the beat, you tell him to go to the rehearsal night, but it's okay, see. You didn't know that cop on the beat. See, you had to get a permit.
Permit. Had you played in any band or anything? Did you play in any band or up there in Assumption Barrett before you came down?

We had three pieces, me and my brother and sister. See, because remember my sister played manly. My sister played manly, my brother played guitar and I played cello. Did your father and your mother play anything? No, my father and my uncle, my father and my brother, he was a little ham fat violin player. And we used to play those, you used to give those warm, see they used to give a dance, they call them balls. They get one big room man and give a dance, 25 cents to come in, see. 15 cents every bite, take it outside, 25 cents if you buy a ticket, double, see. And sell the wine and the gum bowls. That was in New Orleans. Outside of New Orleans.
Outside of New Orleans.

That's the way they do it. They did that up there. See, they had chewing gum at a table, you take a pack of chewing gum and you split it, take it down, see. And you had bananas, you had orange. Now you had to play a march. Whenever you catch that flow of crowd you play a march. You stop playing like you be playing a number. And she hold on your arm and march it right to that table. Any kind of thing in six eight moving for a march, you know. Now whatever she pick up you got to pay for it. See? Now a piece of gum, see some of the dances was 25 cents for a piece of gum. Bananas was 25 cents. Remember one slice of the gum, one slice was nickel or dime, see. Orange, 25 cents. That's right. 15 cents. That's right. See? You pick up it. Now you catch the flow. Now the guys used to watch the dance, the flow would get crowded right after you would play that march. You'd go play it and get the flow crowded. See, just up to the band and march, say she ain't going to turn you loose. She'd go hold on your arm and watch. That's right.
See?

Now there's something else some guys didn't know. Yeah. We had to play all that. We had to play saloon, pokers, mazookas and all that stuff. Chardis. Chardis. Chardis. Chardis. Chardis. Now you tell some of the guys about saloon, pokers right now, they don't know what you're talking about. Tim, look back in your auto language matches, man. You see all that stuff back in there. That's right, yeah.
Different tempo.

Then they come up with a number they call it, the Chicago Glide. Now you had your music to that. Now whatever dance that people danced by, you had your music, they had their music to play that dance. And they'd dance. See? They'd dance. And you had to play them waltzes. The mirror with the waltzes, all those waltzes. See? And you better play the waltzes at the right tempo, because them dancers would tell you. See? When I come out here, they had guys that used to introduce the dance, tell you what to dance. But in New Orleans there was no dance. You had to play the routine of the dancers. The waltzes. Because every dancer had to play the waltzes, the charges. I was wondering about what other music you heard up in the country.
Did they ever have brass bands up there, parades?

Well, the brass bands made more money in them days, and the orchestra made it these days. But they played at funerals. They had parades all through the week. See? Because back in them days they'd bury people on Sunday any other day, didn't they? Because now they tell me they all don't bury on Sunday no more. Sometimes, not all the time.
Sometimes they're better than what they do.

With music? Yeah. They still had music in New Orleans. I saw one last summer. Yeah. See now. The Eureka plays them. Yeah. You see, with the brass bands up here, see they had the guy with the stick. And it was awful funny.

See? Because I started out on the tuba with the music. See? And the last I played in 28, I was writing this very time here. I left Los Angeles playing tuba. And then tuba. Went on the tuba. Went on through. That's when I left the band in Chicago. That's where Johnny had all those kids and women to stay in Chicago. When the name was up on the wall, when they get out of you and get a job. But they want me to stay there. I said no man, you can't take care of me. So I had a job at St. Louis. I went on with Duke Jackson. I stayed with him from September until February. Then Louis Russell sent sent for me. They had sent for me. But too much of that. But Johnny, the guy had all that booking around there. He wouldn't give me the telegram. I sent a telegram to him, but he wouldn't give it to me. Until he and his wife got assaulted, then he'd give me the telegram. See?
I was going to ask him more about that early music up in the country. Because not very many people remember much about that.
Was there much church music up there? No, we played dance music.
I mean, in singing, did you belong in the church in those days? Which church?
Catholic church, that's all. I never knew nothing but Catholic. No Catholic?
Yeah.
No Catholic. Yeah. I never knew nothing but Catholic.
I thought some of the other churches had a lot of singing, you know, spirituals and all that in their churches, like the Baptist.

No, you see the bands, Louis in the late days come out with playing the Saints and all that stuff. But the Saints, they played that when it was going to the funeral with a body. We played hymns, we played them hymns, we didn't do that back in those days. And anybody will tell you that they did back in those days, they tell you something that I don't know about it. Yeah.
He got to Chicago.

Because we were on the river boats. I think you're right. I want to ask you a question. See, because they left that, in 1919 of that, that summer. Because they left around the same time we left. Because Mutt and them left with a short in it. I'll tell you where you get through. Yeah.
So anyway.
Well, I'm asking, I'm asking a question. See, when we .
So when you got that date on the . . .
I quit the boat and come out here in 22. Over in the center for me out here in 22. Yeah.
That's when you played tuba for a while then out here. No, no.
I played tuba here for a while. Did I have a tuba when I first came out here? Yeah. I had my tuba. I had a brass tuba. The same tuba that I sold it to Albert Morgan.
Then you went back to the boat after you'd been here in 22. Is that right? No.

Let me see what did I do. 22. I went back and joined Charlotte Crispin. I left here and went to St. Louis. I joined Charlotte Crispin. Then in 23, I joined the quit Charlotte Crispin band and went with Dewey Jackson band on the boat back to New Orleans. 24, I came on back to St. Louis. Left St. Louis, went on back to New Orleans, joined City Days Band. Still was sitting in the Daz Bean Band until 27. Mudd Carey said for me to come back out here to join him, where he was in Chicago. See?
Yeah, that's that picture where you were playing tuba.

Then I played for the Elves Parade. I was at a convention in Chicago. And I went on to Chicago. Passed through St. Louis, told Dewey I'd be back. That's when Johnny wanted me to stay with him. With all them kids. See? I joined the Drew Jackson band and stayed with the Drew Jackson band then from September 28th until February 29th. I went to the Louis Russell band. I stayed with Louis Russell. That fills that. I stayed with Louis Russell until 1940. That's when Joe fired the whole band for the Chief of Band. He got them kids out of Philadelphia.
I was going to ask about your very first records. Were you on an old record that Fate Marable made with Sidney Dez Bean and Amos White? No.
You weren't on that? I was on that.
Which were your first records? Were you on the Charlie Crust?

Yeah, I was on the Charlie Crust with Dewey Jackson. We made records so safe then, Amos White. See, I was on the boat long for them guys. Amos White. Them guys come on the boat way late. When we first went to St. Louis, the white around St. Louis didn't think Cullors could play no music. That's how bad it was on St. Louis. We had guards, the gardeners around that music stand for the whole summer we was up there.
I heard Baby and all of them talking about it too.

We didn't know it. We just thought the guys would stand around the stand. We didn't know it. We didn't know nothing to laugh. We hear it's laughter. You don't put enough whiskey in it. We're not supposed to have a song. That's going on there, man. You don't put enough whiskey in it. That's going on there. That's going on there. That's going on there. That's not right. That's the sport to have it weak anyway then. Oh, that's all right. I didn't think of anything else to ask you really, Pops. I mean, it's wonderful all the things you've told us already.
Well, we've covered a lot of stuff . Well, this one thing I want to tell you.

I gotta give a lot of credit to my wife. More credit to my wife than I do myself. Because I was, I got so bad drinking for a while, a little drink that I did to, I was forgetting how to come home. I was bad. She fought with me. She stopped me from gambling. She would laugh at me. When I lose and bore me, when I win, well I just win away from it.
Yeah, I guess we've all wasted a lot of money there.

And I tried to give up the things a good way for the guys didn't get away from New Orleans and I tried to remember them, all the old guys that I can remember in books and things that didn't get a chance for these days. And I'm lucky enough to get a chance for just like when I went overseas. I got a chance in my older days. I did all my, it looked like I didn't move my loan traveling in my older days. See? I was running yet? Yeah, we talked about China. And I got to give all the credit to my wife because she got me of the kings.
You let up my your friend, my man, that's the only man, and I was going to supper and drum about it one time. I don't know that one day. Tell them now.

And I don't want to get my own and there. You know the word Bo need a horse. That's what we called it. Always. Always. Huh? And we had some very good times together. We played with some of the best guys together. He got me on some of the best jobs that I could play on in New Orleans. And we had to do it. We played for the cream with the crocks on it. That's all I could say. We did.
Are you saying about the trombone and trumpet?
Did you ever see him play the trombone and trumpet together? Well, I liked him.

I had never seen him play his trombone and trumpet, but I know I liked his trumpet playing. And don't forget that violin. He played violin. And he played a whole lot of piano. All the piano he played, you want to hear. I've heard him do that.
Yeah, I see.

Because spots he played on, Jelly Roll couldn't play that. And I'm not talking to him. I'm not talking to him. I'm talking to all the loud chords. Because he was back there on some good jobs when Tony Jackson and Georgia Thomas and them didn't have nothing to do. Black Pete and all those guys. U. L. Wilson. Albert Cowell. What's this other guy named? Or lived up on Broadway. Alfred Wilson. Alfred Wilson. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. As a king. Yeah. That's all.

They played a lot of jobs down there. Had a lot of pimples. Of course, they gave up music playing out much and devoting themselves. For 40 years. Teaching. They passed. Taught a lot of good. Well, the days.
What's the day of the month?
This is 24th, I believe. When did I see him?
Between what?

We were, you mean two days ago? Yeah. Three days ago. It was about the 20th, I guess. When was that? Thursday. Thursday. We got in Wednesday and we were too tired to go there the first night, so we went the second night. I think it was about the 21st, then we went to the hangover.
What day was he was on the boat? What day was he was on the boat? 23? I don't know about it. 23. I think you figured that out the other day we were talking about.
The first time I saw him since then.
That many years.
Yeah, 20.
That's a long time. Well, I think we covered everything here. We might as well turn it off and get dinner in about ready. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Photographs: Fate Marable boat band, Zurich poster, Louis Russell band, Ralph Sutton
segments.summary: Looking through Foster's photos and posters from the boat band, the 1951 Zurich date, the Louis Russell band and recording sessions in New York.

segments.title: Photographs: a visiting New Orleans trombonist and Foster's pneumonia
segments.summary: Photos of a big-chief trombonist visiting New York and of Foster after his hospital stay with pneumonia.

segments.title: Photographs of Louis Armstrong's weddings and wives
segments.summary: Foster says he was best man at an Armstrong wedding and sorts out Daisy, Lil and later wives from newspaper photos.

segments.title: Scrapbook: 1948 tour tickets, press mix-up about his illness, old letters

segments.summary: Foster says few New Orleans drummers could fit any band and praises John Vigne's shuffle beat.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, players and halls
segments.title: Older bass players: Kimball, Glennie and John Prudence

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, players and halls

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, players and halls

segments.summary: A circus band meant you had to read; Foster admires George (Baquet) and the top men in a touring show band.

segments.summary: Interviewers and Foster try to recall the drummer who preceded Cantrell, and a job played with Buddy.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, players and halls

segments.summary: Foster says only a few bands had regular jobs, the downtown bands working the district at Huntsnagle's, and describes hiring and firing by letter.

segments.summary: Details of who drummed for Superior and Olympia bands, and Foster's moving between jobs and dances.

segments.summary: Where and when quadrilles were played, the split between early-evening and after-midnight crowds.

segments.title: Rough uptown halls and trumpeters Harrison Gougie and Ogin
segments.summary: Foster describes the Funky Butt, Big Easy and Number 12 halls and trumpeters Harrison Gougie and Ogin.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, players and halls
segments.title: Bunk Johnson's decline, his rediscovery in 1937 and the horn
segments.summary: Foster explains how drinking ruined Bunk, how he barely recognized Bunk in 1937, and who bought Bunk his horn.

segments.title: Leaving New Orleans with Louis, paper sack and cotton drawers
segments.summary: Foster tells how he and Louie left home together with almost nothing to go north to Rock Island.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, players and halls
segments.title: The first musicians' local in New Orleans and John Robichaux
segments.summary: Foster does not remember the early local, said to date to around 1900; the interviewer mentions Robichaux and dressing neatly.

segments.title: Moving to New Orleans: Octavia Street and schooling
segments.summary: Foster's mother takes him to New Orleans to work for the Willman family; they live on Octavia Street and he attends school uptown.

segments.title: Baseball and neglecting school for music
segments.summary: Foster tells of catching and hitting a home run, school friends who went on to be Bunk and Eddie, and why he did not want his grandchildren to study music in school.

segments.title: First instruments: cello at seven, a bass from his brother
segments.summary: Foster started on a cello standing on a box, then his brother bought him a string bass; no mandolin or guitar first.

segments.title: The Rozeal band with Roy Palmer and Joe Johnson
segments.summary: Foster's first small band, with guitarists who became trombone and trumpet players.

segments.title: The Magnolia band and rehearsals as parties
segments.summary: Foster joins the Magnolia band and describes rehearsals with food, dancing and the police permit.

segments.title: Country dances up the river: family trio, balls and marches
segments.summary: Playing as a trio with his brother and sister, the ball tradition with gum and bananas sold on a march, and the dance repertoire.

segments.title: Brass bands and funerals; Foster's tuba playing to 1928
segments.summary: Brass bands made the money and played funerals; Foster later played tuba and why he could not fake on it, then left Chicago for Duke Jackson in St. Louis and Louis Russell.

segments.title: Church music and how 'The Saints' was played at funerals
segments.summary: Foster was only Catholic and says dance bands did not play hymns; Saints was slow funeral music in early days.

segments.title: The district as a sideline; picnics and country jobs
segments.summary: Foster says downtown bands held the work, the district was a sideline, and describes freelancing at picnics.

segments.title: The 'bunk cave' banquets with free food and wine
segments.summary: The banquet tradition, with free food and drink, as at Perseverance Hall; the last one played with Manuel around 1909-10.

segments.title: Economy Hall, Francs Amis, Biloxi picnics and visiting bands
segments.summary: Playing Economy Hall was like Carnegie Hall to them; Francs Amis and Biloxi picnics, with bands visiting each other during intermission.

segments.title: Lake camp jobs and guitarists of the Superior and Imperial bands
segments.summary: The all-night camp jobs, and who played guitar, drums and bass in the Superior, Imperial, Olympia and McNeil bands.

segments.title: Storyville seen from a New York question
segments.summary: Foster says he did not know the name Storyville and had to ask where Mahogany Hall was.

segments.title: Learning bass from Manuel; solos began on the boat
segments.summary: Foster says he learned from the leaders he worked with, and Manuel taught him a first number note by note on the Fate Marable boat.

segments.title: Bowing versus plucking and teaching bassists in New York
segments.summary: Slow numbers were bowed, fast ones picked; Foster describes teaching bass students and hardening fingertips.

segments.title: Picking with two fingers for volume and tone
segments.summary: Foster picks with the first two fingers together for volume and grips the strings for tone.

segments.title: Three-, four- and five-string basses and pedal notes
segments.summary: The range of strings and pedal notes on his four-string bass, why high C strings lose bass volume, and five-string basses.

segments.title: Playing by head, not rehearsal, and stock arrangements
segments.summary: Foster's ideas come while playing; stock arrangements all sound alike, and a Louis Russell band story about tempo.

segments.title: Aluminum bass, flat versus round back, amplifying the bass
segments.summary: Foster had the first metal bass and discusses tone, flat-back basses and putting a mic on the bass.

segments.title: Photos of grandchildren and Christmas
segments.summary: Foster shows pictures of his grandchildren, one named for him.

segments.title: His current bass: London three-legged bridge, string height and gut strings
segments.summary: A bass bought in 1939 with a metal bridge from London, string height, and the gut and wound strings he uses.

segments.title: First three-string basses and who had four strings
segments.summary: Foster recalls early New Orleans bassists having three-string basses, with Jimmy Brown the one with four.

segments.title: Learning from a pianist's chords and standing near the piano
segments.summary: Foster says he learned more from one pianist than any other, and prefers to stand next to the piano.

segments.title: Bass placement on the bandstand and the f-hole
segments.summary: Why Foster stands on a certain side of the band so the bass sound carries.

segments.title: Photos of the 1948 France tour and Queen Mary birthday party
segments.summary: Pictures from the Queen Mary and the 1948 tour with Emmett Berry, plus a birthday party on the ship.

segments.title: Playing a solid two, bass as the left hand of the piano
segments.summary: Foster explains his rhythm of a solid two, why drummers dislike it, and how it sounds like a full four.

segments.title: Proving his two-beat bass to symphony bassists
segments.summary: A symphony bassist doubts Foster's rhythm, and Foster offers to prove it with a piano player; he says he took the rhythm from a pianist's left hand.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: Thinking of chords and reading ahead
segments.summary: Foster does not think of chord names; he reads bars ahead and ideas come as he plays.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: Staying modest, and how music was fun in the old days
segments.summary: Foster warns young players not to get big heads and says the old New Orleans players enjoyed music more.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: No union, subbing and a Tuxedo band job anecdote
segments.summary: Bands were strict, there was no union in the early days, and Foster tells of covering jobs between two bands.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: Photo and party chatter: Edmund Hall, Jimmy Archey, Louis's family
segments.summary: The interviewers and Foster identify people in photos and talk about who is touring.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: New York's hard-nosed scene; Bunk, the Eagle Band and Bolden's band
segments.summary: Foster says New York drops players, as with Bunk, and discusses the Eagle Band's poor reading and Bolden band members.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: The old days were better; copying Louis and having your own style
segments.summary: Foster compares old whiskey and bands to today's, says Louis ruined trumpet players who copied his sound, and lists players with individual styles.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: String bass versus tuba for a small band
segments.summary: Foster prefers the string bass for sustain, says the tuba belongs in brass bands, and explains why he took up tuba.

segments.chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
segments.title: Why Foster avoids bass solos and prefers rhythm
segments.summary: Bass solos lack foundation; Foster plays running chords and says dancers follow rhythm.

segments.title: Mahogany Hall Stomp with Louis and Foster's favorite record
segments.summary: Foster recalls recording one number all day with Louis, which made the string bass famous, and names it his favorite record.

segments.title: Too many notes: clarinet and trumpet playing today
segments.summary: Foster dislikes high-register clarinet and too many notes, and praises low-register players like Tio and Pete Fountain.

segments.title: 'Dixieland' versus jazz and ragtime; sharing sheet music
segments.summary: New Orleans bought music from St. Louis publishers, and downtown bands pooled money and exchanged books.

segments.title: Uptown bands and how Johnny Brown became a clarinetist
segments.summary: A few uptown bands and players are recalled, and Foster tells how he found a clarinetist and brought him into a band.

segments.chapter: Youth and day jobs in New Orleans
segments.title: Where he lived, the McCall family and his grandmother
segments.summary: Foster lived with his mother on the Willman premises; the McCalls' mother played piano, and his grandmother raised him.

segments.chapter: Youth and day jobs in New Orleans
segments.title: Day jobs: coal wagon alongside Louis Armstrong and long-shore work
segments.summary: Foster and Louis both drove coal wagons; he held several day jobs while playing every night.

segments.summary: Foster says current drummers are cymbal beaters, praises early New Orleans drummers and stresses tuning.

segments.title: Zutty Singleton and Paul Barbarin, and being fired from a show band
segments.summary: Foster tells how Zutty replaced Barbarin in a band, and Zutty's too-fast tempos.

segments.summary: The group clarifies that Manuel Manetta was called Bonito because people could not say Manetta.

segments.title: How George Foster became 'Pops'
segments.summary: Foster says he and Louis started calling each other Pops in New York and the name stuck on records.

segments.title: Piano versus guitar in the rhythm section; Bernard Addison
segments.summary: Foster prefers piano now since few guitarists play chords, praises one guitarist and recalls New Orleans pianist-guitarists.

segments.summary: Foster dislikes banjo and electric guitar and describes a recording box that gave a full bass tone in France.

segments.title: Slapping the bass versus snapping the strings
segments.summary: Foster explains how often he slaps, how he lets the string ring, and chat about a recent set.

segments.summary: Foster and the interviewers discuss the Los Angeles Black and Tan band, its trumpeter and players, and Oliver not being first.

segments.summary: Foster lists leaving the boat for the coast in 1922, St. Louis, Creath, Dewey Jackson, Chicago and Louis Russell until 1940.

segments.summary: Foster says he was on the Creath records, and recalls guards at the bandstand in St. Louis.

segments.summary: Foster credits his wife for stopping his drinking and gambling, which let him tour overseas in later years.

segments.summary: Foster praises a friend who played trumpet, trombone, violin and piano and got him good jobs, with other pianists named.
